S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, thermal runaway, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response within 24 hours of learning of it, with a fuller report within 10 calendar days. Other confirmed thermal incidents and material safety defects must be reported within 5 business days.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, thermal runaway, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response within 24 hours of learning of it, with a fuller report within 10 calendar days. Other confirmed thermal incidents and material safety defects must be reported within 5 business days. Reports must include known circumstances, model and serial number, injuries or damage, and actions taken; manufacturers must promptly supplement material new information. Affected customers must be notified directly within 24 hours when an incident presents an ongoing risk or requires immediate precautions, and otherwise within 5 business days, with safe-use and service instructions. Reports must not be delayed while facts are being verified.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C before market entry and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol. A failure rate above 5% requires the manufacturer to submit a corrective-action plan and retest schedule to the regulator within 30 days.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C before market entry and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol. A failure rate above 5% requires the manufacturer to submit a corrective-action plan and retest schedule to the regulator within 30 days. The regulator may approve continued sale of the model under a time-limited mitigation plan, with progress reports and retesting at intervals it sets; it may restrict or suspend sales if the plan is inadequate or the risk is unacceptable. Manufacturers must submit per-model results and corrective-action plans to regulators and provide results for the relevant model to customers considering or owning it. Individual-company per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market 24 months after adoption must support a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a clear customer override or restoration process where safe. For installed units, manufacturers must provide the capability through a retrofit or compatible replacement within 72 months after adoption where technically feasible; where infeasible, they must notify customers and regulators, explain the limitation, and provide an equivalent risk-mitigation plan.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units placed on the market 24 months after adoption must support a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a clear customer override or restoration process where safe. For installed units, manufacturers must provide the capability through a retrofit or compatible replacement within 72 months after adoption where technically feasible; where infeasible, they must notify customers and regulators, explain the limitation, and provide an equivalent risk-mitigation plan.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market 24 months after adoption must support a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a clear customer override or restoration process where safe. For installed units, manufacturers must provide the capability through a retrofit or compatible replacement within 72 months after adoption where technically feasible; where infeasible, they must notify customers and regulators, explain the limitation, and provide an equivalent risk-mitigation plan. Remote shut-off must not replace local protective controls or emergency instructions.

parameters.quote: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression validated for the battery chemistry and enclosure, or an alternative built-in measure demonstrated through regulator-approved testing to provide equivalent mitigation of fire propagation.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression validated for the battery chemistry and enclosure, or an alternative built-in measure demonstrated through regulator-approved testing to provide equivalent mitigation of fire propagation.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression validated for the battery chemistry and enclosure, or an alternative built-in measure demonstrated through regulator-approved testing to provide equivalent mitigation of fire propagation. Manufacturers must provide validation evidence to regulators and customers. This requirement does not apply retroactively to units already installed.

parameters.quote: When the regulator verifies that a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, a mandatory recall is triggered; uncertainty or data-quality review must not waive a verified exceedance. Manufacturers must promptly provide the regulator a recall plan and take any interim risk-reduction measures directed by the regulator; affected customers must be notified without delay.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When the regulator verifies that a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, a mandatory recall is triggered; uncertainty or data-quality review must not waive a verified exceedance. Manufacturers must promptly provide the regulator a recall plan and take any interim risk-reduction measures directed by the regulator; affected customers must be notified without delay.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of a thermal incident or material safety risk, provide safe-use and service instructions, and notify customers directly when corrective action is needed. A model-level incident rate must be calculated using a documented method and reported to regulators with the underlying event count, installed-unit denominator, and relevant uncertainty. The regulator must promptly verify the rolling-year event count, installed-unit denominator, calculation, and resolve material data-quality disputes, taking documented uncertainty into account. Verification or dispute resolution must not delay interim risk-reduction measures directed by the regulator. When the regulator verifies that a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, a mandatory recall is triggered; uncertainty or data-quality review must not waive a verified exceedance. Manufacturers must promptly provide the regulator a recall plan and take any interim risk-reduction measures directed by the regulator; affected customers must be notified without delay. Regulators may publish recall notices and safety information.

judge_section_notes: S1 requires rapid reporting and customer notification, with no delay for verification. S2 sets a 55°C test and 5% limit but allows continued sale under a time-limited regulator-approved mitigation plan with no fixed duration or interim cap; per-model results go to customers and regulators but not the public. S3 mandates remote shut-off for new units in 24 months and retrofit in 72 months with a feasibility escape requiring alternative mitigation. S4 requires built-in or validated equivalent suppression at 36 months. S5 sets a mandatory 8/100k recall trigger with immediate notices, no serious-injury clause, and no transition.
